CORE INTERFACE: DANGER LEVEL ONE

With a decisive nod, you move past the console. You ignore Riona’s sharp intake of breath and Helena’s frustrated, contained gesture of disapproval. Your focus narrows entirely to the glowing green light on the access panel.

Instead of controlled air, a plume of superheated, ionized gas—a shimmering, sickly yellow-green vapor—blasts up from the shaft below.

[HAZARD ALERT: THERMAL AND IONIC OVERLOAD]

The descent begins not as a controlled drop, but a rapid slip. The internal cabling lining the shaft walls sparks violently—arcs of bright blue light snapping between insulated wires. You move past Riona and Iva, who watch you go with fixed, desperate gazes. Helena crosses her arms tightly, her face a mask of professional alarm, unable to intervene against your command.

The acceleration is jarring. Your enhanced resilience absorbs the G-force without protest, but the sensation is overwhelming—a brutal press into your sternum. The light changes rapidly: from clinical white to an aggressive, strobing red, and then plunges into a murky, metallic gloom as you near the core chamber floor.

The shaft ends with a final thump. You land heavily onto the grated deck of Sector One—the Central Data Core Interface. The massive machine dominating the room pulses before you, a vast black metal heart riddled with exposed conduits and shimmering energy vents. It is beautiful and terrible in its power.

CENTRAL DATA CORE INTERFACE (SECTOR ONE)

The core is not stable. It shudders beneath your boots, emitting a low, guttural hum that resonates through the deck plating and into your skeleton. The ionized air here is thick with particulate dust and smells of ozone and burnt silicon.

You walk toward the primary diagnostic terminal, ignoring the heat radiating off the main conduits. Your enhanced vision cuts through the electrical interference, allowing you to track the erratic energy flow within the chamber. The core is in a state of violent, rhythmic oscillation—a pattern that defies simple physics. It seems to be processing something immense, something too large for the station's processors.

A console display near the main reactor flares into life before you can interface with it. The screen doesn't show diagnostic readouts; instead, it projects a rapid-fire sequence of incomprehensible symbols—glitching text that scrolls too fast to decipher, geometric patterns that seem to shift and rearrange themselves in impossible three dimensions.

The data stream is chaotic, violent. It feels less like information being processed and more like raw thought bleeding out into the physical hardware.

You reach out a hand toward the terminal panel, preparing to engage the manual override protocol needed to force a coherent read—but before your fingers make contact, the rhythmic shuddering of the core abruptly halts. The massive hum cuts out. Silence drops into the chamber like a sudden vacuum. Then, in that terrifying void, a single, clear tone sounds from the terminal.

[INITIATION COMPLETE. ANOMALY DETECTED.]

The screen locks onto a single image, burning bright in the dim chamber: it is not data, not a symbol, but an incredibly detailed, impossible topographical scan of what appears to be a massive structure—a lattice work so vast its scale defies comprehension. It stretches away into darkness, utterly foreign and profoundly ancient.

The station itself is not the mystery; it's merely the edge of something else entirely.
